# Introduction

Probabilistic modelling provides answer to the quintessential question of probability theory: "What is the probability of an event". In classroom setting, the answer is typically a single number which is deduced from modelling assumptions. For instance, we may assume that we roll a perfectly symmetrical dice or, that subsequent coin flips are identical. In practical applications, however, the question to quantify probability is often asked \emph{repeatedly} with varying context. One naturally expects that the answer will vary depending on the context. For instance, a bank may wonder what is the probability that the borrower will repay a loan. The context could be provided by the current financial disclosure of the borrower's assets. To answer the question it is customary to build a mathematical model.

There is a multitude of ways to build different models, and thus one may wonder which models are good, or perhaps even which one in a set of models is the best. Historically, the question gained attention in the context of weather forecasting. Since early 20th century weather forecasts are typically are probabilistic. An easy way to check how good a weather forecasters (or more precisely their models) are, is to compare them with climate observations. Climate is computed by taking the expected frequency over long-term (one or more years). If the probability of rain on any given day in a year is 40%, we can compare that with the average probability that was provided by the forecaster throughout the whole year. For a good forecaster, they should be pretty close.

There is an even finer method to compare forecast's fidelity. We can subdivide the probability interval $[0,1]$ into (nonintersecting) subintervals. For each subinterval, we compare the observed frequency of rain on days when the forecast fell into it. Suppose for instance that one the subintervals was $I = [0.45, 0.55]$. We would expect that the probability $p$ of rain on days when forecast fell into $I$ would be around 0.5 A model that matches this expectation reasonably well is said to be *well-calibrated*. An example of real-world diagram that checks for calibration is in

![Example of weather calibration](BrierExample.png)

Good calibration of a probabilistic model is a very desirable property.

# Logistic models

A model can viewed as an algorithm, whose input is the context, and the output is the desired probability. Mathematical representation of context is a vector. It maybe called vector of features, if features were handpicked, or the embedding vector, if the vector is produced by a neural network. By a logistic model we mean an algorithm that for a given context vector $\mathbf{x}$ outputs the probability $$
p(\mathbf{x}) = \sigma(\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x}),\quad\textrm{where } \sigma(x) = \frac{\exp x}{1 + \exp{x}}.
$$ {#eq-logistic} Note that we have $$
\begin{aligned}
\lim_{x\rightarrow-\infty} \sigma(x) = 0, \quad \textrm{and}\quad
\lim_{x\rightarrow\infty} \sigma(x) = 1
\end{aligned},
$$ {#eq-logistic2} and thus this model allows predicting probabilities in the whole range $(0,1)$.

The two principal examples of logistic models are linear discriminant analysis and logistic regression. They both have form @eq-logistic, but they differ in the method they use to estimate the weight vector $\mathbf{w}$. Logistic regression is more commonly used, but they are considered to give approximately the same results. We can illustrate it on the famous iris dataset. The iris dataset was created in 1930's by Edgar Anderson, an American botanist. It contains four measurements (features) of three iris species

-   iris versicolor L.,
-   iris virginica L.,
-   iris setosa.

From statistical point of view the important property of the dataset is that the features are approximately normally distributed. Let us illustrate this by comparing the distributions of one the measurements (the width of petal) as shown in @fig-density.

```{r}
#| label: fig-density
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Class-conditional densities of Petal.Width for versicolor and virginica (kernel density estimate)
#| dev: !expr if (knitr::is_latex_output()) "tikz" else "png"
#| fig-ext: !expr if (knitr::is_latex_output()) "tex" else "png"

## In the PDF/LaTeX render, use tikzDevice so all plot text (including the
## legend's p-hat) is typeset by the actual LaTeX engine -- a real \hat{p}
## rather than R plotmath's approximation. Other formats keep plotmath.
if (knitr::is_latex_output()) {
  suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(tikzDevice))
}

d0 <- droplevels(subset(iris, Species %in% c("versicolor", "virginica")))

col_versicolor <- "#1b9e77"
col_virginica  <- "#d95f02"

dens_versicolor <- density(d0$Petal.Width[d0$Species == "versicolor"])
dens_virginica  <- density(d0$Petal.Width[d0$Species == "virginica"])

par(mar = c(4, 4.5, 3, 1))
plot(dens_versicolor, col = col_versicolor, lwd = 2,
     xlim = range(d0$Petal.Width),
     ylim = c(0, max(dens_versicolor$y, dens_virginica$y)),
     xlab = "Petal.Width", ylab = "Density", main = "")
lines(dens_virginica, col = col_virginica, lwd = 2, lty = 2)

rug(d0$Petal.Width[d0$Species == "versicolor"], col = paste0(col_versicolor, "99"))
rug(d0$Petal.Width[d0$Species == "virginica"], side = 3, col = paste0(col_virginica, "99"))

  c("$\\hat{p}(\\mathrm{versicolor})$", "$\\hat{p}(\\mathrm{virginica})$")
} else {
```

The results are shown in @fig-chunk1. They include Bayes classifier $$
\hat p(virginica | x) = \frac{\hat p(x \mid virginica)P(virginica)}{\hat p(x \mid virginica)P(virginica)+ \hat p(x \mid versicolor)P(versicolor)}
$$

```{r }
#| label: fig-chunk1
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Comparison of LDA and logistic regression on iris dataset
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(MASS))

d <- droplevels(subset(iris, Species %in% c("versicolor", "virginica")))
d$y <- as.integer(d$Species == "virginica")

lda_fit <- lda(Species ~ Petal.Width, data = d)
glm_fit <- glm(y ~ Petal.Width, data = d, family = binomial)

xg <- seq(min(d$Petal.Width), max(d$Petal.Width), length.out = 400)

p_lda <- predict(lda_fit, newdata = data.frame(Petal.Width = xg))$posterior[, "virginica"]
p_glm <- predict(glm_fit, newdata = data.frame(Petal.Width = xg), type = "response")

## Nonparametric ("plug-in") Bayes classifier: estimate each class-conditional
## density via KDE, then combine via Bayes' rule (equal priors, n = 50 each).
dens_versicolor <- density(d$Petal.Width[d$Species == "versicolor"])
dens_virginica  <- density(d$Petal.Width[d$Species == "virginica"])
f_versicolor <- approxfun(dens_versicolor$x, dens_versicolor$y, rule = 2)
f_virginica  <- approxfun(dens_virginica$x, dens_virginica$y, rule = 2)
p_bayes <- f_virginica(xg) / (f_versicolor(xg) + f_virginica(xg))

col_lda   <- "#1b9e77"
col_glm   <- "#d95f02"
col_bayes <- "#7570b3"

par(mar = c(4, 4.5, 3, 1))
plot(xg, p_lda, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = col_lda, yaxt = "n",
     xlab = "Petal.Width", ylab = "P(virginica | Petal.Width)",
     main = "", ylim = c(0, 1))
lines(xg, p_glm, lwd = 2, lty = 2, col = col_glm)
lines(xg, p_bayes, lwd = 2, lty = 3, col = col_bayes)

## y-axis on [0,1], tick labels to 1 decimal place
y_ticks <- seq(0, 1, by = 0.2)
axis(2, at = y_ticks, labels = sprintf("%.1f", y_ticks), las = 1)

## Maximal gap between the two predicted curves, marked with a vertical
## segment capped by small horizontal ticks at each end (a "dimension line").
gap <- abs(p_lda - p_glm)
i_max <- which.max(gap)
x_max <- xg[i_max]
y_lo <- min(p_lda[i_max], p_glm[i_max])
y_hi <- max(p_lda[i_max], p_glm[i_max])

arrows(x0 = x_max, y0 = y_lo, x1 = x_max, y1 = y_hi,
       code = 3, angle = 90, length = 0.05, lwd = 1.5, col = "black")
text(x_max, (y_lo + y_hi) / 2, sprintf("max gap = %.2f", gap[i_max]), pos = 2, cex = 0.85)

legend("bottomright", bty = "n", legend = c("LDA", "Logistic regression", "Bayes (KDE plug-in)"),
       col = c(col_lda, col_glm, col_bayes), lwd = 2, lty = c(1, 2, 3))
```

Interestingly, we couldn't carry out the comparison for virginica and setosa samples because the fitting procedure for logistic regression will not converge. Let us examine the reason. Logistic regression model is fitted by maximizing the likelihood on the dataset with features $\mathbf{x_i}$ and provided labels $y_i$. In our case $$
\overbrace{L(w, b)}^{\textrm{likelihood function}} = \prod_i \left\{ \sigma(wx_i + b)\ \ \ \ \mathrm{ when  }\ y_i = virginica \atop 1 - \sigma(wx_i + b)\ \mathrm{ when  }\ y_i = versicolor \right\}.
$$ The key fact that the ranges of petal width do not intersect (the data is linearly separable), as seen from summary statistics for each species shown in @tbl-petalwidth. For any $\lambda$ we have $$
\begin{aligned}
\lambda (x_i - 1) > 0 \quad y_i = virginica\\
\lambda (x_i - 1) < 0 \quad y_i = setosa
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-logistic3} Thus if we choose $w = \lambda$ and $b = -\lambda$ and let $\lambda \rightarrow \infty$, we see that $L(w, b)$ will approach 1 arbitrarily close. However it will never exactly one, since for any $x$ the logistic function $\sigma(x) < 1$.

<!-- @tbl-petalwidth shows the range (minimum and maximum) of petal width for each of the three species. -->

```{r}
#| label: tbl-petalwidth
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: Range of Petal.Width (cm) by species
species_levels <- levels(iris$Species)
petal_width_tab <- data.frame(
  Species = species_levels,
  Count = sapply(species_levels, function(s) 
    sum(iris$Species == s)),
  Min  = sapply(species_levels, function(s) min(iris$Petal.Width[iris$Species == s])),
  Max  = sapply(species_levels, function(s) max(iris$Petal.Width[iris$Species == s])),
  Mean = sapply(species_levels, function(s) mean(iris$Petal.Width[iris$Species == s])),
  SD   = sapply(species_levels, function(s) sd(iris$Petal.Width[iris$Species == s]))
)
## Two-line header only renders reliably in HTML; fall back to a plain
## single-line label for docx/jats so the pipe-table syntax isn't broken.
sd_label <- if (knitr::is_html_output()) "Standard<br>Deviation" else "Standard Deviation"
knitr::kable(petal_width_tab, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE, escape = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Species", "Count", "Min", "Max", "Mean", sd_label))
```

<!-- Since the ranges do not intersect, it is possible to fit model so that probabilities at dataset points are arbitrarily close to the true values zero and one. -->

This problem does not occur with LDA. Fitting LDA can be done in either of two ways

-   by maximizing Fisher discriminant ratio for vector $\mathbf{w}$, or
-   by maximum likelihood method where the parameters are the means $\mu_1, \mu_2$ and joint covariance matrix $\Sigma$ which form a generative model of data points $(\mathbf{x}_i, y_i)$.

When using the first approach, the existence of the optimal $\mathbf{w}$ is assured by the fact that Fisher discriminant ratio is the same for collinear vectors, and thus follows from the fact that a continuous function always attains a maximum on a sphere, a compact set.

This argument will not work for logistic regression, since the objective, the expected likelihood $L(\mathbf{w}, b)$ is *not* invariant to rescaling the model's coefficients.

An observant reader may point out that we just need more samples. Indeed, Gaussian distribution has infinite support and thus under Gaussian assumption on the distribution of the variate for both classes if we take enough samples, the ranges will intersect. The probability of the intersection can be computed exactly using order statistics. Suppose we draw $n$ samples per class, and let $F_s$, and $F_v$, $f_v$ denote the distribution functions of the two classes and the density of the second class. The setosa range $[\min_i X_i, \max_i X_i]$ fails to intersect the virginica range precisely when $\max_i X_i < \min_j Y_j$ (the reverse ordering has negligible probability, as setosa's mean lies far below virginica's). Conditioning on the position of the minimum $\min_j Y_j$, whose density is $n\,(1-F_v(t))^{n-1} f_v(t)$, and using independence of the two samples, $$
P\left(\max_i X_i < \min_j Y_j\right) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} F_s(t)^n \; n\,\bigl(1-F_v(t)\bigr)^{n-1} f_v(t)\, dt.
$$ Evaluating this integral numerically with the plug-in parameters from @tbl-petalwidth (setosa: $\mu = 0.25$, $\sigma = 0.11$; virginica: $\mu = 2.03$, $\sigma = 0.27$) and solving for the sample size at which it drops to $1/2$ shows that one would need $n \approx 464\,000$ samples *per class* before the ranges have at least a 50% chance to intersect. The intuition for this enormous number is that the two means are more than six pooled standard deviations apart, so an intersection requires a joint extreme-tail event. Another way is needed. We will provide several alternatives in the next section.

# Regularization of logistic regression

T

```{r}
#| label: load-calibration-ratios
#| echo: false
#| include: false
ratios_df <- read.csv(path.expand("~/ams/calibration_ratios.csv"))
M_reps <- length(unique(ratios_df$rep))
```

To compare how well each regularized model recovers the true class probability, we ran a Monte Carlo simulation with $M=`r M_reps`$ replications: repeatedly sampling $N=50$ points per class from two unit-variance Normal distributions with means 6 apart, fitting L1-penalized logistic regression, L2-penalized logistic regression, Firth logistic regression, Platt scaling, Platt scaling with halved pseudocounts ("2N" targets), and LDA to each sample, and recording, at every sampled point, the ratio of each model's predicted to the true (Bayes-optimal) probability of being class B. @fig-one-dataset-predictions shows what a single replication looks like: the predicted-probability curve from each of the six models, together with the true Bayes curve, fitted to one simulated dataset. @fig-calibration-ratios then shows the resulting distribution of $\log_{10}(\hat{p}/p_{\text{true}})$ for each method, restricted to points sampled from class A; a value of 0 indicates perfect calibration at that point, positive values indicate the model overestimated the true probability, and negative values indicate underestimation. We restrict to class-A points because $p_{\text{true}}$ is bounded away from $1$ there: class A sits 6 SDs from class B, so $p_{\text{true}}$ only approaches $1$ for a class-A point that is itself several SDs from its own mean, which essentially never happens. Class-B points, by contrast, almost always have $p_{\text{true}} \approx 1$, where $\log p$ is insensitive to the model's actual log-odds and the ratio is uninformative regardless of how wrong the model is. Nothing is lost by dropping class-B points: the whole setup — both Gaussians and all six fitting procedures — is symmetric under swapping the class labels and reflecting $x$ about the midpoint, so class-A and class-B behavior are mirror images in distribution. Because the two class means are 6 SDs apart, the two classes end up linearly separable in $x$ (some threshold perfectly splits class A from class B) in the large majority of replications; in that regime, weakly-regularized models can drive predicted probabilities toward 0/1, showing up here as strongly negative log-ratios.

```{r}
#| label: fig-one-dataset-predictions
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Predicted P(class B | x) from each of the six models, together with the true Bayes-optimal probability, for a single simulated dataset (the first of the M Monte Carlo replications used in @fig-calibration-ratios below). Tick marks along the bottom show the sampled class A (dark) and class B (light) points.
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(glmnet)
  library(logistf)
})

set.seed(1)   # same seed as simulate_calibration_ratios.R -> reproduces its first replication
n   <- 50
mu1 <- 0; mu2 <- 6; sdv <- 1

x1 <- rnorm(n, mu1, sdv)
x2 <- rnorm(n, mu2, sdv)
x  <- c(x1, x2)
y  <- factor(rep(c("A", "B"), each = n))
yb <- as.integer(y == "B")

xg <- seq(min(x) - 1, max(x) + 1, length.out = 400)

## True Bayes-optimal probability curve (same closed form as in
## simulate_calibration_ratios.R).
b_true <- (mu2 - mu1) / sdv^2
a_true <- -(mu2^2 - mu1^2) / (2 * sdv^2)
p_true <- plogis(a_true + b_true * xg)

## L1 / L2 penalized logistic regression.
x_mean <- mean(x); x_sd <- sd(x)
X  <- cbind((x  - x_mean) / x_sd, 0)
Xg <- cbind((xg - x_mean) / x_sd, 0)
cv_l2 <- cv.glmnet(X, y, family = "binomial", alpha = 0, standardize = FALSE)
cv_l1 <- cv.glmnet(X, y, family = "binomial", alpha = 1, standardize = FALSE)
p_l2 <- as.numeric(predict(cv_l2, newx = Xg, s = "lambda.min", type = "response"))
p_l1 <- as.numeric(predict(cv_l1, newx = Xg, s = "lambda.min", type = "response"))

## Firth logistic regression.
firth_fit <- logistf(yb ~ x, pl = FALSE)
p_firth <- plogis(coef(firth_fit)[1] + coef(firth_fit)[2] * xg)

## Platt scaling (standard and 2N-target variant).
Np <- sum(yb == 1); Nn <- sum(yb == 0)
t_std <- ifelse(yb == 1, (Np + 1) / (Np + 2), 1 / (Nn + 2))
t_2N  <- ifelse(yb == 1, (2 * Np + 1) / (2 * Np + 2), 1 / (2 * Nn + 2))
p_platt  <- predict(suppressWarnings(glm(t_std ~ x, family = binomial)),
                     newdata = data.frame(x = xg), type = "response")
p_platt2 <- predict(suppressWarnings(glm(t_2N ~ x, family = binomial)),
                     newdata = data.frame(x = xg), type = "response")

## LDA (pooled-variance closed form, as in simulate_calibration_ratios.R).
m1 <- mean(x1); m2 <- mean(x2)
s2_pooled <- ((n - 1) * var(x1) + (n - 1) * var(x2)) / (2 * n - 2)
b_lda <- (m2 - m1) / s2_pooled
a_lda <- -(m2^2 - m1^2) / (2 * s2_pooled)
p_lda <- plogis(a_lda + b_lda * xg)

curves <- list(L1 = p_l1, L2 = p_l2, Firth = p_firth,
               Platt = p_platt, Platt_2N = p_platt2, LDA = p_lda)
cols <- c(L1 = "#1b9e77", L2 = "#d95f02", Firth = "#7570b3",
          Platt = "#e7298a", Platt_2N = "#66a61e", LDA = "#e6ab02")
labs <- c(L1 = "L1 logistic", L2 = "L2 logistic", Firth = "Firth logistic",
          Platt = "Platt scaling", Platt_2N = "Platt (2N targets)", LDA = "LDA")

par(mar = c(4, 4.5, 1, 1))
plot(xg, p_true, type = "l", lwd = 3, col = "black",
     xlab = "x", ylab = "P(class B | x)", ylim = c(0, 1))
for (mdl in names(curves)) {
  lines(xg, curves[[mdl]], lwd = 2, col = cols[mdl])
}
rug(x1, col = "grey30")
rug(x2, col = "grey60")

legend("bottomright", bty = "n",
       legend = c("True (Bayes)", unname(labs[names(curves)])),
       col = c("black", unname(cols[names(curves)])), lwd = c(3, rep(2, 6)))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-calibration-ratios
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Distribution of log10(predicted probability / true probability) for each regularization method, restricted to class-A points and pooled across all Monte Carlo replications. The dashed red line marks perfect calibration (ratio = 1).
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6
model_order  <- c("L1", "L2", "Firth", "Platt", "Platt_2N", "LDA")
model_labels <- c(L1 = "L1 logistic", L2 = "L2 logistic", Firth = "Firth logistic",
                  Platt = "Platt scaling", Platt_2N = "Platt (2N targets)", LDA = "LDA")

par(mfrow = c(2, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
for (m in model_order) {
  log_ratio <- ratios_df$log10_ratio[ratios_df$model == m & ratios_df$class == "A"]
  h <- hist(log_ratio, breaks = 40, plot = FALSE)
  ymax <- max(h$density) * 1.15

  hist(log_ratio, breaks = h$breaks, freq = FALSE, col = "grey85", border = "white",
       xlab = "log10(predicted prob / true prob)", ylim = c(0, ymax),
       main = unname(model_labels[m]))
  abline(v = 0, col = "red", lwd = 2, lty = 2)

  ## Small downward arrow at the mean, roughly mid-height, labeled above it.
  m_val <- mean(log_ratio)
  y_top <- ymax * 0.65
  y_bot <- ymax * 0.45
  arrows(x0 = m_val, y0 = y_top, x1 = m_val, y1 = y_bot,
         col = "blue", lwd = 2, length = 0.08)
  text(m_val, y_top, sprintf("mean=%.1f", m_val), col = "blue", pos = 3, cex = 0.85)
}
```

# Applications

## Multi-class classification via pairwise coupling

The models discussed so far are inherently binary. A standard way to extend a binary classifier to $K > 2$ classes is to fit a model on every pair of classes and then *couple* the $\binom{K}{2}$ pairwise probability estimates into a single probability vector over all $K$ classes. We illustrate this with a three-class problem: three bivariate Normal populations with identity covariance ($\mathrm{sd}=1$ in each coordinate) and means forming a right triangle with sides $9$, $12$, $15$ (the $3$-$4$-$5$ triple scaled by $3$), with the right angle at class 1's mean and $150$ points sampled per class. Because the classes have equal priors and identity covariance, the exact Bayes-optimal rule is the nearest-mean classifier, giving us a ground truth to compare against.

For every one of the three class pairs we fit a Firth (bias-reduced) logistic regression, generalizing the one-dimensional Firth fit used earlier in this paper to a two-dimensional design matrix via the same modified-score IRLS iteration. The three pairwise fits are then combined into one three-class probability vector two different ways: the fixed-point iteration of Wu, Lin and Weng (2004) — the same algorithm libsvm uses to turn one-vs-one SVM outputs into multi-class probabilities — and the earlier pairwise-coupling algorithm of Hastie and Tibshirani (1998) that WLW's method was designed to improve on. We also compute the exact Bayes-optimal classifier from the true generating means for comparison.

Both coupling algorithms recover the Bayes decision boundaries closely near the training data, with only small, expected deviations far from all three means, where the pairwise Firth fits are extrapolating. @fig-ht-argmax shows the argmax decision regions under Hastie-Tibshirani coupling, representative of both methods, with the true Bayes boundary overlaid (dashed).

![Firth logistic regression + Hastie-Tibshirani coupling: argmax decision regions, with the true Bayes boundary overlaid (dashed).](three_class_ht_coupling_argmax.png){#fig-ht-argmax}

## Partial pairwise coupling

Wu-Lin-Weng coupling finds the probability vector $p$ minimizing $L(p) = \sum_{i<j}(r_{ji}\,p_i - r_{ij}\,p_j)^2$, a sum over all $\binom{3}{2}=3$ pairwise terms. To see how much any single pairwise comparison actually contributes to the final decision regions, we solve the same fixed-point iteration with one term dropped entirely from the objective — the corresponding pairwise Firth fit is still computed but never enters the coupling step — giving three "partial coupling" variants, one for each pair that can be dropped.

@fig-partial-coupling shows the argmax regions for all three partial-coupling variants alongside the full three-term coupling as a reference. Dropping the pair $(i,j)$ predictably degrades the boundary specifically between classes $i$ and $j$ (since the coupling step no longer sees that pairwise comparison directly, only indirectly through the other two pairs), while leaving the region boundaries involving the third class comparatively unaffected.

::: {#fig-partial-coupling layout-ncol=2}
![Full coupling (reference)](three_class_firth_full_wlw_argmax_reference.png){#fig-partial-full}

![Drop pair (1,2)](three_class_firth_partial_wlw_drop12_argmax.png){#fig-partial-drop12}

![Drop pair (1,3)](three_class_firth_partial_wlw_drop13_argmax.png){#fig-partial-drop13}

![Drop pair (2,3)](three_class_firth_partial_wlw_drop23_argmax.png){#fig-partial-drop23}

Argmax decision regions under full (3-term) Wu-Lin-Weng coupling versus dropping one pairwise term from the coupling objective, with the true Bayes boundary overlaid (dashed).
:::
